claim: Fructophily is a rare trait that consists of the preference for fructose over other carbon sources.
source: Fructophily is a rare trait that consists of the preference for fructose over other carbon sources.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations to prior work on fructophily.

claim: In a yeast lineage (the Wickerhamiella/Starmerella, W/S clade) comprised of fructophilic species thriving in the high-sugar floral niche, the acquisition of fructophily is concurrent with a wider remodeling of central carbon metabolism.
source: Here, we show that in a yeast lineage (the Wickerhamiella/Starmerella, W/S clade) comprised of fructophilic species thriving in the high-sugar floral niche, the acquisition of fructophily is concurrent with a wider remodeling of central carbon metabolism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by comparative genomics and experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is evidence for the loss of alcoholic fermentation in an ancestor of the W/S clade.
source: Coupling comparative genomics with biochemical and genetic approaches, we gathered ample evidence for the loss of alcoholic fermentation in an ancestor of the W/S clade and subsequent reinstatement through either horizontal acquisition of homologous bacterial genes or modification of a pre-existing yeast gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative genomic analysis showing absence of native ADH1 and PDC1 genes, phylogenetic evidence, and identification of C. galacta lacking these genes.

claim: Alcoholic fermentation was subsequently reinstated in the W/S clade through either horizontal acquisition of homologous bacterial genes or modification of a pre-existing yeast gene.
source: Coupling comparative genomics with biochemical and genetic approaches, we gathered ample evidence for the loss of alcoholic fermentation in an ancestor of the W/S clade and subsequent reinstatement through either horizontal acquisition of homologous bacterial genes or modification of a pre-existing yeast gene.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic evidence showing bacterial origin of ADH1 genes and functional characterization of ARO10 in St. bombicola.

claim: An enzyme required for sucrose assimilation was acquired from bacteria in the W/S clade.
source: An enzyme required for sucrose assimilation was also acquired from bacteria, suggesting that the genetic novelties identified in the W/S clade may be related to adaptation to the high-sugar environment.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis of SUC2 and experimental demonstration that the suc2Δ mutant cannot grow on sucrose.

claim: The genetic novelties identified in the W/S clade may be related to adaptation to the high-sugar environment.
source: An enzyme required for sucrose assimilation was also acquired from bacteria, suggesting that the genetic novelties identified in the W/S clade may be related to adaptation to the high-sugar environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ecological niche (floral nectar) and the suite of acquired genes.

claim: Central carbon metabolism can be remodeled by a surge of HGT events.
source: This work shows how even central carbon metabolism can be remodeled by a surge of HGT events.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the specific findings about the W/S clade.

claim: Horizontal gene transfers (HGT) are thought to have played a very important role in domestication.
source: For example, horizontal gene transfers (HGT) are thought to have played a very important role in domestication (Gibbons et al., 2012; Marsit et al., 2015; Ropars et al., 2015) and in the evolution of metabolism in fungi (Alexander et al., 2016; Wisecaver and Rokas, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Horizontal gene transfers (HGT) have played a very important role in the evolution of metabolism in fungi.
source: For example, horizontal gene transfers (HGT) are thought to have played a very important role in domestication (Gibbons et al., 2012; Marsit et al., 2015; Ropars et al., 2015) and in the evolution of metabolism in fungi (Alexander et al., 2016; Wisecaver and Rokas, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a high frequency of HGT events involving gene clusters related to fungal primary and secondary metabolism.
source: Instances of the latter are best showcased by the high frequency of HGT events involving gene clusters related to fungal primary and secondary metabolism (Campbell et al., 2012; Khaldi and Wolfe, 2011; Slot and Rokas, 2010; 2011; Wisecaver and Rokas, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genes encoding nutrient transporters seem to be among the most frequently transferred in horizontal gene transfer.
source: When considering the horizontal transfer of single genes, those encoding nutrient transporters seem to be among the most frequently transferred (Coelho et al., 2013; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Richards, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HGTs are often associated with rapid adaptation to new environments.
source: However, available evidence suggests that HGTs are often associated with rapid adaptation to new environments (Cheeseman et al., 2014; Gojković et al., 2004; Qiu et al., 2013; Richards et al., 2011; Richards and Talbot, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ffz1 is a unique, high-capacity, specific fructose transporter intimately associated with fructophilic metabolism in ascomycetous budding yeasts.
source: In line with these findings, we recently reported on the evolutionary history of a unique, high-capacity, specific fructose transporter, Ffz1, which is intimately associated with fructophilic metabolism in ascomycetous budding yeasts (subphylum Saccharomycotina) (Gonçalves et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The evolution of FFZ1 involved the likely horizontal acquisition of the gene from filamentous fungi by the most recent common ancestor of a lineage in the Saccharomycotina composed of fructophilic yeasts.
source: The evolution of FFZ1 involved the likely horizontal acquisition of the gene from filamentous fungi (subphylum Pezizomycotina) by the most recent common ancestor (MRCA) of a lineage in the Saccharomycotina, composed so far entirely of fructophilic yeasts (Gonçalves et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Most of the approximately one hundred species forming the W/S clade are associated with the floral niche and are often isolated from fructose-rich nectar.
source: Most of the approximately one hundred species forming this clade (Wickerhamiella and Starmerella genera, as well as closely related Candida species), are associated with the floral niche and are often isolated from fructose-rich nectar (Canto et al., 2017; de Vega et al., 2017; Lachance et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fructophilic lactic acid bacteria populate the floral niche.
source: Interestingly, fructophilic lactic acid bacteria, whose metabolism has been dissected in detail, also populate the floral niche (Endo et al., 2009; Endo and Salminen, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fructophilic lactic acid bacteria grow poorly on glucose, which can be at least partly explained by their lack of respiratory chain enzymes and alcohol dehydrogenase activity.
source: These bacteria have been shown to grow poorly on glucose, which can be at least partly explained by their lack of respiratory chain enzymes and alcohol dehydrogenase activity, deficiencies that hinder NAD+ regeneration during growth on this sugar, as shown for Lactobacillus kunkei (Maeno et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In fructophilic bacteria, fructose can be used both as a carbon source and as an electron acceptor for the re-oxidation of NAD(P)H.
source: In contrast to glucose, fructose can be used both as a carbon source and as an electron acceptor for the re-oxidation of NAD(P)H (Zaunmüller et al., 2006), providing an explanation of why it is favored over glucose.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Fructophily in lactic acid bacteria seems to be linked to redox homeostasis.
source: Hence, fructophily in lactic acid bacteria seems to be linked to redox homeostasis (Endo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Fructophilic yeasts grow vigorously on glucose when it is the only carbon and energy source available.
source: In yeasts, it is still unclear how preferential consumption of fructose may be beneficial, partly because unlike fructophilic bacteria, fructophilic yeasts grow vigorously on glucose when it is the only carbon and energy source available (Sousa-Dias et al., 1996; Tofalo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A strict correlation was found between the presence of Ffz1 and fructophily in all species investigated.
source: Our previous work suggested that, although a strict correlation was found so far between the presence of Ffz1 and fructophily in all species investigated (Cabral et al., 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Leandro et al., 2014) and the requirement for FFZ1 was genetically confirmed in the fructophilic species Zygosaccharomyces rouxii (Leandro et al., 2014), it is very likely that there are additional requirements for fructophily.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The requirement for FFZ1 was genetically confirmed in the fructophilic species Zygosaccharomyces rouxii.
source: Our previous work suggested that, although a strict correlation was found so far between the presence of Ffz1 and fructophily in all species investigated (Cabral et al., 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Leandro et al., 2014) and the requirement for FFZ1 was genetically confirmed in the fructophilic species Zygosaccharomyces rouxii (Leandro et al., 2014), it is very likely that there are additional requirements for fructophily.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There are likely additional requirements for fructophily beyond the FFZ1 gene.
source: Our previous work suggested that, although a strict correlation was found so far between the presence of Ffz1 and fructophily in all species investigated (Cabral et al., 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2016; Leandro et al., 2014) and the requirement for FFZ1 was genetically confirmed in the fructophilic species Zygosaccharomyces rouxii (Leandro et al., 2014), it is very likely that there are additional requirements for fructophily.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work and the motivation for the current study.

claim: The FFZ1 gene does not seem to be sufficient to impart a fructophilic character to a previously glucophilic species.
source: Thus, the FFZ1 gene does not seem to be sufficient to impart a fructophilic character to a previously glucophilic species.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior work.

claim: Fructophilic behavior was completely abolished in the ffz1∆ mutant of Starmerella bombicola.
source: The sugar-consumption profile in YP medium supplemented with 10% (w/v) fructose and 10% (w/v) glucose (conditions where fructophily is apparent, hereafter referred to as 20FG medium), showed that fructophilic behavior was completely abolished in the ffz1∆ mutant (Figure 1), similarly to what was found in Z. rouxii (Leandro et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A slight increase in the glucose consumption rate was observed for the ffz1∆ mutant compared to the wild type when cultures were grown in 20FG medium.
source: A slight increase in the glucose consumption rate was also observed for the ffz1∆ mutant compared to the wild type when cultures were grown in 20FG medium (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Some W/S-clade yeasts were previously known to be efficient producers of sugar alcohols or lipids to the detriment of ethanol.
source: On the other hand, some W/S-clade yeasts were previously known to be efficient producers of sugar alcohols or lipids to the detriment of ethanol (Magyar and Tóth, 2011;Lee et al., 2003a; Kurtzman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the ADH1 gene encodes the enzyme mainly responsible for the conversion of acetaldehyde into ethanol.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the ADH1 gene encodes the enzyme mainly responsible for the conversion of acetaldehyde into ethanol (de Smidt et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Predicted Adh1 proteins retrieved from W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were much less similar to the S. cerevisiae ADH1 query than the genes recovered from non-fructophilic counterparts.
source: Notably, while the phylogenetic distance between all the species surveyed and S. cerevisiae was similar, protein sequence identity, E-value, and bitscore values denoted that predicted Adh1 proteins retrieved from W/S-clade species and C. infanticola as top hits of the tBLASTx search were much less similar to the S. cerevisiae ADH1 query than the genes recovered from their non-fructophilic counterparts Sugiyamaella lignohabitans, Blastobotrys adeninivorans, and Yarrowia lipolytica (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When Adh1 protein sequences from W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were used as queries in BLASTp searches, the top 1000 hits consisted entirely of bacterial proteins.
source: Moreover, when Adh1 protein sequences from W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were used as queries in BLASTp searches in the NCBI non-redundant (nr) database, the top 1000 hits consisted entirely of bacterial proteins, while when Adh1 sequences of Su. lignohabitans, B. adeninivorans, and Y. lipolytica yeasts were similarly employed as queries, the top 1000 hits recovered were fungal proteins.
evidence: This is supported by BLASTp search results.

claim: When Adh1 sequences of Su. lignohabitans, B. adeninivorans, and Y. lipolytica yeasts were used as queries in BLASTp searches, the top 1000 hits recovered were fungal proteins.
source: Moreover, when Adh1 protein sequences from W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were used as queries in BLASTp searches in the NCBI non-redundant (nr) database, the top 1000 hits consisted entirely of bacterial proteins, while when Adh1 sequences of Su. lignohabitans, B. adeninivorans, and Y. lipolytica yeasts were similarly employed as queries, the top 1000 hits recovered were fungal proteins.
evidence: This is supported by BLASTp search results.

claim: W/S-clade species and C. infanticola have Adh1 homologs of bacterial origin.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that W/S-clade species and C. infanticola have Adh1 homologs of bacterial origin, in contrast to the remaining three species.
evidence: This is an inference based on BLAST results.

claim: The Pdc sequences retrieved from the genomes of W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were more dissimilar to S. cerevisiae Pdc1 than those recovered from the three remaining non-fructophilic species.
source: Remarkably, the Pdc sequences retrieved in this manner from the genomes of W/S-clade species and C. infanticola were also found to be more dissimilar to S. cerevisiae Pdc1 than those recovered from the three remaining non-fructophilic species, based on sequence identity, E-values, and bitscores (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Two out of the three Pdc sequences identified in C. versatilis were more closely related to bacterial Pdc proteins than to fungal Pdc enzymes.
source: In line with the observations for Adh1 sequences, two out of the three Pdc sequences identified in C. versatilis, were more closely related to bacterial Pdc proteins than to fungal Pdc enzymes (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Pdc orthologs found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola seem to belong to a decarboxylase family that is phylogenetically related to S. cerevisiae Aro10.
source: In this case, the lower E-value appears to reflect the fact that the Pdc orthologs found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola seem to belong to a decarboxylase family that is phylogenetically related to S. cerevisiae Aro10.
evidence: This is an inference based on BLAST results and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, Aro10 acts preferentially on substrates other than pyruvate and is not involved in alcoholic fermentation.
source: In S. cerevisiae, Aro10 acts preferentially on substrates other than pyruvate and is not involved in alcoholic fermentation (Kneen et al., 2011; Romagnoli et al., 2012; Vuralhan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The phylogeny confirmed the clustering of the W/S-clade sequences with Aro10 proteins from fungi, which indicates that PDC1 was lost in the W/S clade.
source: This phylogeny (Figure 3A and B) confirmed the clustering of the W/S-clade sequences with Aro10 proteins from fungi, which indicates that PDC1 was lost in the W/S clade.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The two Pdc1-like proteins from C. versatilis were clustered with bacterial pyruvate decarboxylases.
source: Additionally, as suggested by the BLASTp results, the two Pdc1-like proteins from C. versatilis were clustered with bacterial pyruvate decarboxylases (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All glycolytic genes were found to be present in the examined species and exhibited the expected level of similarity to S. cerevisiae query proteins.
source: All glycolytic genes were examined in the same set of species and were all found to be present and to exhibit the expected level of similarity to S. cerevisiae query proteins (Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: It is very unlikely that alcoholic fermentation genes were missed in W/S-clade species because of insufficient coverage or quality of the genome assemblies used.
source: This, together with the fact that other inspected publicly available genome assemblies of W/S-clade species are of very high quality (e.g. Wickerhamiella domercqiae JCM 9478, PRJDB3620 or St. bombicola JCM 9596 from RIKEN Center), makes it very unlikely that alcoholic fermentation genes were missed in W/S-clade species because of insufficient coverage or quality of the genome assemblies used.
evidence: This is an inference based on genome quality assessment.

claim: A considerably larger number of genes of bacterial origin was found in W/S-clade species and C. infanticola when compared with the two species more distantly related to the W/S clade.
source: We found a considerably larger number of genes of bacterial origin in W/S-clade species and also in C. infanticola when compared with the two species more distantly related to the W/S clade (Su. lignohabitans and B. adeninivorans, Figure 2A, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by Alien Index analysis results shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: C. versatilis displayed the highest number of putative HGT-derived genes from bacteria (211).
source: Notably, C. versatilis displayed the highest number of putative HGT-derived genes from bacteria (211), followed by W. domercqiae with 80 genes for which phylogenetic clustering with bacteria could be confirmed (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Alien Index analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A surge of HGT events occurred in the MRCA of the W/S clade.
source: Given that all W/S-clade species possess a higher number of HGT-derived genes when compared to their closest relatives, it is possible that a surge of HGT events occurred in the MRCA of the W/S clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of HGT-derived genes across species.

claim: 52 ortholog groups with representatives in two or more W/S-clade genomes were defined.
source: Indeed, after implementation of alignment thresholds (protein sequences > 150 amino acids) and collapsing the replicate phylogenies and lineage-specific gene duplications, it was possible to define 52 ortholog groups with representatives in two or more W/S-clade genomes.
evidence: This is supported by the HGT detection pipeline results.

claim: Different W/S-clade species subsequently retained different sets of genes after the surge of HGT events.
source: Not excluding the possibility that independent events also occurred in the various species, this suggests that a surge of HGT events took place in the MRCA of the W/S clade and that different species subsequently retained different sets of genes, C. versatilis being the species that retained the most genes of bacterial origin (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of HGT-derived genes across species.

claim: The horizontally transferred invertase appears to be the only enzyme with sucrose-hydrolyzing capacity encoded in the W/S-clade genomes investigated.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the MAL and the IMA genes have also been shown to play a role in sucrose hydrolysis (Deng et al., 2014; Voordeckers et al., 2012), but these genes are absent in the genomes of W/S-clade species, meaning that the horizontally transferred invertase appears to be the only enzyme with sucrose-hydrolyzing capacity encoded in the W/S-clade genomes investigated.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis and citations.

claim: Strong support for clustering of W/S-clade sequences to Acetobacteraceae SacC sequences was observed in the phylogenetic tree.
source: In a phylogenetic tree reconstructed using the 200 top phmmer hits to W/S-clade species Candida magnoliae (protein ID 2301, see Figure 2—source data 2), strong support for clustering of W/S-clade sequences to Acetobacteraceae SacC sequences was observed (Figure 4A and Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: A topology comparison test strongly supported the HGT hypothesis for SUC2.
source: A topology comparison test (Approximately Unbiased, AU) also strongly supported the HGT hypothesis (p-value=4e−07).
evidence: This is supported by statistical topology test results.

claim: Out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity and peroxidase activity.
source: Notably, out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity (GO:0016491 and GO:0016616, 14 genes) and peroxidase activity (GO:004601, two genes), while a BLAST KOALA annotation (Kanehisa et al., 2016) indicated that the biological processes most frequently involved were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by GO annotation analysis.

claim: The biological processes most frequently involved in the 52 ortholog groups were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins.
source: Notably, out of 43 proteins to which a GO molecular function was assigned, 16 impacted redox homeostasis and were associated with oxidoreductase activity (GO:0016491 and GO:0016616, 14 genes) and peroxidase activity (GO:004601, two genes), while a BLAST KOALA annotation (Kanehisa et al., 2016) indicated that the biological processes most frequently involved were amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and metabolism of cofactors and vitamins (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by BLAST KOALA annotation analysis.

claim: In addition to ADH1, other alcohol dehydrogenase genes seem to have been horizontally acquired by W/S-clade species, including putative ADH6 and SFA1 orthologs.
source: We noted that, in addition to ADH1, other alcohol dehydrogenase genes seem to have been horizontally acquired by W/S-clade species (Figure 2—source data 4), including putative ADH6 and SFA1 orthologs, which can also participate in alcoholic fermentation in S. cerevisiae (Drewke et al., 1990; Ida et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by HGT detection analysis and citations.

claim: In all cases except for SFA1, the 'native' yeast orthologs appear to have been lost in W/S-clade genomes.
source: In all cases, except for SFA1, the 'native' yeast orthologs appear to have been lost in W/S-clade genomes.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomic analysis.

claim: All W/S-clade species clustered with strong support with the Acetobacteraceae Adh1 proteins.
source: The resulting Adh1 tree (Figure 5A) included protein sequences from both bacteria and fungi. All W/S-clade species clustered with strong support with the Acetobacteraceae (Proteobacteria) Adh1 proteins (Figure 5A and Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Within the Adh1 W/S-clade cluster, the overall phylogenetic relationships were in line with the expected relationships between the species, suggesting that a single HGT event occurred in the MRCA of this clade.
source: Within the Adh1 W/S-clade cluster, the overall phylogenetic relationships were in line with the expected relationships between the species (Figure 2A), suggesting that a single HGT event occurred in the MRCA of this clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Topology comparison tests strongly supported the Adh1 HGT event to the W/S clade.
source: Topology comparison tests (AU) strongly supported the Adh1 HGT event to the W/S clade (p-value=8e−03), adding to the strong evidence of HGT provided by the robustly supported branch that clusters the W/S-clade xenologs with bacteria and the AI results.
evidence: This is supported by statistical topology test results.

claim: The two Adh1 sequences from C. infanticola are not similar to those of the W/S clade.
source: However, the two Adh1 sequences from C. infanticola are not similar to those of the W/S clade (Figure 5C), as might be expected if a single HGT event were responsible for the acquisition of the ADH1 gene in both lineages.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: C. infanticola Adh1 sequences grouped with Adh1 sequences from the distantly related Lactobacillales and Enterobacteriales, implying that an independent HGT event may have occurred in the C. infanticola lineage.
source: These sequences instead grouped, albeit with weak support, with Adh1 sequences from the distantly related Lactobacillales and Enterobacteriales (Figure 5C), implying that an independent HGT event may have occurred in the C. infanticola lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: W/S-clade sequences clustered with strong support with Proteobacteria Adh6 sequences.
source: In this phylogeny, W/S-clade sequences clustered with strong support (>95%) with Proteobacteria Adh6 sequences, within a large cluster that also encompasses known fungal Adh6 proteins.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: While Adh1 W/S-clade sequences grouped with those of the Acetobacteraceae, the Adh6 sequences are more closely related to those of other bacterial families.
source: Remarkably, while Adh1 W/S-clade sequences grouped with those of the Acetobacteraceae (Figure 5A and Figure 5B), the Adh6 sequences are more closely related to those of other bacterial families, as highlighted in Figure 6B.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The absence of an ADH6 ortholog in C. infanticola was confirmed by a tBLASTx search.
source: The absence of an ADH6 ortholog was further confirmed by a tBLASTx search against the C. infanticola genome using Adh6 sequences from both S. cerevisiae (KZV09178.1) and St. bombicola as queries.
evidence: This is supported by tBLASTx search results.

claim: Both ADH1 and ADH6 were lost in an ancestor of C. infanticola and the W/S clade.
source: This result suggests that both ADH1 and ADH6 were lost in an ancestor of C. infanticola and the W/S clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of ADH6 in C. infanticola and the presence of bacterial versions in the W/S clade.

claim: The ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species.
source: Interestingly, the ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species (Figure 6A, Figure 6B and Figure 2—source data 4), and Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most paralogs (four in total).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most ADH6 paralogs (four in total).
source: Interestingly, the ADH6 xenologs were apparently duplicated several times within each W/S-clade species (Figure 6A, Figure 6B and Figure 2—source data 4), and Starmerella bacillaris and C. magnoliae harbor the most paralogs (four in total).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source.
source: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source and have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars, meaning that ethanol production in aerated batch cultures starts only when cell densities are very high,limiting oxygen availability (typically OD640 nm 30,~5–10 g/L ethanol in St. bombicola).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: W/S-clade species have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars.
source: All W/S-clade species tested were capable of using ethanol as carbon and energy source and have a Crabtree-negative behavior when growing on sugars, meaning that ethanol production in aerated batch cultures starts only when cell densities are very high,limiting oxygen availability (typically OD640 nm 30,~5–10 g/L ethanol in St. bombicola).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: In all non-W/S-clade species tested, the characteristic NADH-dependent Adh activity was readily observed, but no NADPH-dependent Adh activity was detected.
source: In all non-W/S-clade species tested, the characteristic NADH-dependent Adh activity was readily observed, but no NADPH-dependent Adh activity was detected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), in line with available information concerning yeast enzymes (Cho and Jeffries, 1998; Dashko et al., 2014; Ganzhorn et al., 1987; Leskovac et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and citations.

claim: All W/S-clade species tested exhibited Adh activity when either NADH or NADPH was added to the reaction mixture.
source: Conversely, all W/S-clade species tested (St. bombicola, C. magnoliae, and St. bacillaris) exhibited Adh activity when either NADH or NADPH was added to the reaction mixture (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: There was a lower affinity for the substrate (higher Km) for NADPH-dependent activity in St. bombicola.
source: In fact, although both cofactors could be used for conversion of acetaldehyde into ethanol, there was a lower affinity for the substrate (higher Km) for NADPH-dependent activity in St. bombicola (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In Acetobacter pasteurianus, alcohol dehydrogenase activity was found to be NADH-dependent.
source: Interestingly, in Acetobacter pasteurianus a bacterial species in the Acetobacteraceae, the same family as the likely donor of W/S-clade Adh1, alcohol dehydrogenase activity was found to be NADH-dependent, although it is unclear whether NADPH was also tested as a cofactor (Masud et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of ADH1 (adh1∆) did not significantly affect specific growth rates in glucose or fructose when compared to the wild type during aerated growth.
source: During aerated growth, deletion of ADH1 (adh1∆) did not seem to significantly affect specific growth rates in glucose or fructose when compared to the wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There was a five-fold decrease in ethanol production in the adh1∆ mutant.
source: However, we noted a five-fold decrease in ethanol production (Figure 7A) and the absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The adh1∆ mutant showed absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source.
source: However, we noted a five-fold decrease in ethanol production (Figure 7A) and the absence of growth on ethanol as sole carbon and energy source in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: No Adh activity was detected in cell-free extracts of the adh1∆ mutant when either NADH or NADPH was used.
source: Although some ethanol was produced, no Adh activity was detected in cell-free extracts of the adh1∆ mutant when either NADH or NADPH was used (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Adh1 is the main enzyme used in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola.
source: These results suggest that Adh1 is the main enzyme used in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that it therefore likely accepts both NADH and NADPH as cofactors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the adh1∆ mutant.

claim: The significant decrease in ethanol yield in the adh1∆ mutant seems to be counterbalanced by a concomitant increase in glycerol production.
source: In line with the cofactor preference measured in cell extracts, the significant decrease in ethanol yield seems to be counterbalanced by a concomitant increase in glycerol production (Figure 7A), similarly to what has been observed in the S. cerevisiae adh1∆ mutant (de Smidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citation.

claim: Growth of the adh1∆ mutant cultivated on identical growth medium but under limited aeration was severely affected.
source: Moreover, growth of the adh1∆ mutant cultivated on identical growth medium but under limited aeration was severely affected (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Adh1 plays an important role in redox homeostasis, namely in NAD+ regeneration in the absence of oxygen.
source: Taken together, these observations strongly suggest that Adh1 plays an important role in redox homeostasis, namely in NAD+ regeneration in the absence of oxygen because, similarly to S. cerevisiae, glycerol formation in St. bombicola is probably a NAD+ regenerating reaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of the adh1∆ mutant and comparison to S. cerevisiae.

claim: NADP+ dependent glycerol dehydrogenase activity was not detected in cell-free extracts of St. bombicola.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we did not detect NADP+ dependent glycerol dehydrogenase activity in cell-free extracts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), and in at least one W/S-clade species, this reaction was shown to be NADH-dependent (Van Bogaert et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D and citation.

claim: Mannitol production was significantly decreased in the adh1∆ mutant.
source: In contrast, mannitol production, which is a NADP+ regenerating reaction (Lee et al., 2003b), was significantly decreased in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and citation.

claim: The deletion of each of the two ADH6 paralogous genes (adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants) did not significantly affect ethanol production.
source: The deletion of each of the two ADH6 paralogous genes (adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants) did not significantly affect ethanol production (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When Adh1 is functional, Adh6a and Adh6b are not essential for ethanol metabolism and are probably mainly involved in other metabolic reactions.
source: This means that, although some of the enzymes encoded by these genes might be involved in the production of ethanol in the absence of Adh1, when Adh1 is functional, they are not essential for ethanol metabolism and are probably mainly involved in other metabolic reactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotypes of the adh6a∆ and adh6b∆ mutants.

claim: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant.
source: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7B), but fructophily was still observed in all mutants and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Fructophily was still observed in all mutants (adh1∆, adh6a∆, and adh6b∆) and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
source: There was a significant decrease in sugar consumption rates in the adh1∆ mutant (Figure 7B), but fructophily was still observed in all mutants and became even more pronounced as the lack of Adh1 affected glucose consumption more than it did fructose consumption.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The aro10Δ mutant failed to produce ethanol.
source: This mutant failed to produce ethanol, as might be expected in the complete absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The aro10Δ mutant exhibited increased glycerol production.
source: Similarly to the adh1Δ mutant, it exhibited increased glycerol production, but unlike the former, it grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and 7C.

claim: The aro10Δ mutant grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions.
source: Similarly to the adh1Δ mutant, it exhibited increased glycerol production, but unlike the former, it grew considerably slower than the wild type strain in aerated conditions (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The decrease in growth rate in the aro10Δ mutant was probably mainly due to the fact that the absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity affects other metabolic routes in addition to alcoholic fermentation, such as the production of acetate and acetoin.
source: This decrease was probably mainly due to the fact that the absence of pyruvate decarboxylase activity affects other metabolic routes in addition to alcoholic fermentation, such as the production of acetate and acetoin (Flikweert et al., 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype and citation to prior literature.

claim: Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola.
source: The phenotype observed in this mutant confirmed that Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that, therefore, the modification of enzymatic specificities was also involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the aro10Δ mutant.

claim: The modification of enzymatic specificities was involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
source: The phenotype observed in this mutant confirmed that Aro10 is the only decarboxylase involved in alcoholic fermentation in St. bombicola and that, therefore, the modification of enzymatic specificities was also involved in remodeling alcoholic fermentation in W/S-clade yeasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phenotype of the aro10Δ mutant and the phylogenetic relationship of Aro10 to S. cerevisiae Aro10.

claim: In the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant.
source: Importantly, in the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant (Figure 7B) and, in fact, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth (Figure 7C), while fructose was almost totally consumed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: In the aro10∆ mutant, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth, while fructose was almost totally consumed.
source: Importantly, in the aro10∆ mutant, glucose consumption seems to be even more seriously affected than in the adh1Δ mutant (Figure 7B) and, in fact, glucose was left all but untouched even after 120 hr of growth (Figure 7C), while fructose was almost totally consumed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: All publicly available genomes across the entire subphylum Saccharomycotina possess at least one ADH1 ortholog.
source: In fact, all publicly available genomes across the entire subphylum Saccharomycotina possess at least one ADH1 ortholog.
evidence: This is based on analysis of publicly available genomes.

claim: Candida galacta lacks both PDC1 and ADH1.
source: Remarkably, sequencing of the genome of Candida galacta (Figure 8) in the context of a distinct project (the Y1000+ Project sequencing the genomes of all known species of Saccharomycotina; http://y1000plus.org)(Hittinger et al., 2015) showed that it lacks both PDC1 and ADH1 (Figure 8, Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by genome sequencing data shown in Figure 8 and Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: The phylogenetic position of C. galacta strongly supports the hypothesis that loss of native ADH1 preceded the acquisition of the bacterial versions of the gene by the C. infanticola lineage and by the MRCA of the W/S clade.
source: The phylogenetic position of this species strongly supports the hypothesis that loss of native ADH1 preceded the (likely independent) acquisition of the bacterial versions of the gene by the C. infanticola lineage and by the MRCA of the W/S clade.
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic position of C. galacta and its lack of ADH1 and PDC1.

claim: The presence of xenologs involved in alcoholic fermentation in extant W/S-clade yeasts can be best explained by the need to restore alcoholic fermentation in a lineage that had previously lost it.
source: In conclusion, given the evidence presented here, the presence of xenologs involved in alcoholic fermentation in extant W/S-clade yeasts can be best explained by the need to restore alcoholic fermentation in a lineage that had previously lost it.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: The involvement of bacterial genes in restoring alcoholic fermentation seems to have been circumstantial and possibly a consequence of the availability of the donor in the same environment.
source: In this case, the involvement of bacterial genes seems to have been circumstantial and possibly a consequence of the availability of the donor in the same environment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the ecological context.

claim: W/S-clade Adh1 proteins are most closely related to those of a bacterial lineage that is also frequently associated with the floral niche (Acetobacteraceae).
source: The ecological opportunity for the horizontal exchange of genetic material underlying the acquisition of bacterial ADH1 seems to have existed for a long time, since W/S-clade Adh1 proteins are most closely related to those of a bacterial lineage that is also frequently associated with the floral niche (Acetobacteraceae) (Iino et al., 2012; Suzuki et al., 2010; Tucker and Fukami, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations about the ecology of Acetobacteraceae.

claim: Evolution of 'native' SUC2 seems to be punctuated by multiple loss events resulting in a patchy extant distribution.
source: Unlike the 'native' version of ADH1, which is ubiquitous in the Saccharomycotina except in the W/S clade, evolution of 'native' SUC2 seems to be punctuated by multiple loss events resulting in a patchy extant distribution (Carlson et al., 1985), which is probably linked to its role as a 'social' gene (Sanchez and Gore, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The basis for fructophily arose in yeasts in a lineage devoid of alcoholic fermentation, but probably well equipped to use fructose as electron acceptor with concomitant production of mannitol.
source: Taken together, our results suggest the enticing hypothesis that the basis for fructophily arose in yeasts in a lineage devoid of alcoholic fermentation, but probably well equipped to use fructose as electron acceptor with concomitant production of mannitol (Baek et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2003a), through the horizontal acquisition of the Ffz1 transporter that enabled the efficient utilization of fructose as carbon and energy source.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the findings of the study and citations.

claim: A putative ancestor lineage would resemble the aro10∆ mutant in that it would be unable to use glucose in high-sugar conditions.
source: Such a lineage would resemble the aro10∆ mutant in that it would be unable to use glucose in high-sugar conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phenotype of the aro10∆ mutant.

claim: The putative ancestor might subsequently have acquired fermentative capacity to enable efficient glucose consumption and SUC2 to permit the utilization of sucrose.
source: This putative ancestor might subsequently have acquired fermentative capacity to enable efficient glucose consumption and SUC2 to permit the utilization of sucrose, thereby completing the set of tools required to use the sugars abundant in the floral niche.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary trajectory.

claim: Fructophilic yeasts seem to have been able to overcome the inability to use glucose efficiently, as observed in extant fructophilic bacteria.
source: In conclusion, our previous (Gonçalves et al., 2016) and present results uncovered, to our knowledge for the first time, an instance of major remodeling of central carbon metabolism in fungi involving the horizontal acquisition of a multitude of genes mostly from bacteria. Thereby, fructophilic yeasts seem to have been able to overcome the inability to use glucose efficiently, as observed in extant fructophilic bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The suc2∆ mutants were unable to grow on sucrose as sole carbon and energy source.
source: Growth assays in medium supplemented with sucrose as sole carbon and energy source, showed that suc2∆ mutants were unable to grow (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), while the wild-type strain attained high-cell densities.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The suc2∆ mutant failed to consume measurable amounts of sucrose, even after 72 hr.
source: Furthermore, the suc2∆ mutant failed to consume measurable amounts of sucrose, even after 72 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: During growth of the wild-type strain on sucrose, the decrease in sucrose concentrations was accompanied by the appearance of fructose and glucose in the growth medium, strongly suggesting that the horizontally transferred SUC2 gene encodes an extracellular invertase.
source: During growth of the wild-type strain on sucrose, the decrease in sucrose concentrations was accompanied by the appearance of fructose and glucose in the growth medium, strongly suggesting that the horizontally transferred SUC2 gene encodes an extracellular invertase (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The apparent absence of genes encoding sucrose transporters in the W/S-clade genomes analyzed indicates that sucrose must be first hydrolyzed outside the cell to be used as a carbon and energy source.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the apparent absence of genes encoding sucrose transporters in the W/S-clade genomes analyzed, which indicates that sucrose must be first hydrolyzed outside the cell to be used as a carbon and energy source.
evidence: This is an inference based on genomic analysis and the experimental results.

claim: St. bombicola is a species used for the production of sophorolipids, which are amphipathic molecules that are employed as biosurfactants.
source: The most prominent example is St. bombicola, a species used for the production of sophorolipids, which are amphipathic molecules that are employed as biosurfactants (Samad et al., 2015; Takahashi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Starmerella bacillaris is often found in wine fermentations and is known for diverting an important fraction of its carbon flux towards the production of glycerol instead of ethanol.
source: Starmerella bacillaris is often found in wine fermentations and is known for diverting an important fraction of its carbon flux towards the production of glycerol instead of ethanol (Englezos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Candida magnoliae has been reported to be capable of producing large amounts of erythritol.
source: Candida magnoliae has been reported to be capable of producing large amounts of erythritol (Ryu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis of a few selected sites was capable of considerably increasing the affinity of S. cerevisiae Aro10 for pyruvate.
source: However, it has been shown that site-directed mutagenesis of a few selected sites was capable of considerably increasing the affinity of S. cerevisiae Aro10 for pyruvate (Kneen et al., 2011), which supports the notion that this shift in substrate specificity may have occurred naturally in the course of evolution of W/S-clade yeasts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss and subsequent reacquisition of a metabolic pathway through multiple HGT events was reported previously for the unicellular red algae Galdieria phlegrea.
source: Loss and subsequent reacquisition of a metabolic pathway through multiple HGT events was reported previously for the unicellular red algae Galdieria phlegrea where massive gene loss occurred concomitantly with adaptation to a specialized niche in the common ancestor of Cyanidiophytina red algae (Qiu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.
